cases.name: document-609
cases.text: A municipal archive that decides to digitise its holdings soon learns that scanning is the easy part. The scanners run day and night, but every page still needs a record that says what it is, where it came from and who may read it. Old ledgers mix several hands on one page, maps were folded and refolded until the creases cut through the street names, and photographs arrive in envelopes whose labels describe a different picture. Cataloguers therefore work in two passes: a quick one that gives every item a stable identifier and a date range, and a slow one that adds the descriptions people actually search for. Search is where the investment pays off or fails. A historian looking for flood damage in the eighteen nineties rarely types the words the clerk used at the time; she asks about water, cellars and repairs, while the ledger speaks of assessments, relief payments and the parish fund. Keyword indexes miss most of those matches. An embedding model that maps the question and the catalogue entry into the same space finds them, because it has learned that the two descriptions are about the same event. The archive does not need the model to be clever, only consistent: the same entry must land in the same place every time it is encoded, on every machine that serves the catalogue, so that a result found last week can be found again today. The pages below are the archive's own log of the figures it was asked about most often. Record 1: bridge repairs changed by 37 percent in district B. cases.text: A municipal archive that decides to digitise its holdings soon learns that scanning is the easy part. The scanners run day and night, but every page still needs a record that says what it is, where it came from and who may read it. Old ledgers mix several hands on one page, maps were folded and refolded until the creases cut through the street names, and photographs arrive in envelopes whose labels describe a different picture. Cataloguers therefore work in two passes: a quick one that gives every item a stable identifier and a date range, and a slow one that adds the descriptions people actually search for. Search is where the investment pays off or fails. A historian looking for flood damage in the eighteen nineties rarely types the words the clerk used at the time; she asks about water, cellars and repairs, while the ledger speaks of assessments, relief payments and the parish fund. Keyword indexes miss most of those matches. An embedding model that maps the question and the catalogue entry into the same space finds them, because it has learned that the two descriptions are about the same event. The archive does not need the model to be clever, only consistent: the same entry must land in the same place every time it is encoded, on every machine that serves the catalogue, so that a result found last week can be found again today.
